title: My Grandson’s Lunch Account Was Short $6. Then I Found 400 Envelopes and an $86,000 Secret at His School (PART 2) – Story Loom
excerpt: …and every single one of those 400 envelopes had the same thing written on the front in neat block letters: “LUNCH FUND DONATION — ANONYMOUS.”
author: admin

blocks.text: …and every single one of those 400 envelopes had the same thing written on the front in neat block letters: “LUNCH FUND DONATION — ANONYMOUS.”

I’d been dropping a twenty into that donation box by the front office every month for six years. So had half the grandparents I knew from church. The school newsletter thanked us every spring: “Thanks to your generosity, no child at Maple Ridge goes hungry.”
And yet my grandson had come home crying because the cafeteria lady told him his account was negative six dollars and he could only have a cheese sandwich. In front of everyone.

I went to the office to pay it, and to ask why the donation fund hadn’t covered him. The receptionist looked confused. “What donation fund?” she said. “We don’t have one. The box is for the PTA bake sale.” Then she frowned and said, “Actually, I don’t know what that box is for. Ms. Reyes empties it.”
Ms. Reyes. Sandra Reyes. The school business manager. My niece. My late sister’s daughter, whom I helped raise after her mother died, whom I recommended for the job in 2018.

I didn’t sleep that night. The next morning I asked the principal, Mr. Okafor, for a meeting. I told him I’d donated about $1,400 over the years and wanted a receipt for taxes. He said there was no record of any lunch donation account in the district system. None.

The district auditor found the envelopes a week later. Sandra had kept them, every single envelope, in a filing box in her office closet, because some of them had names and checks and she needed them to cash the checks into a “Maple Ridge Student Support” account she had opened herself at a different bank. Four hundred envelopes. Six years. $86,000.
Meanwhile, the real lunch debt at the school had grown to $11,300. Kids had been getting the cheese sandwich for years. Kids whose grandparents thought they were feeding them.

Sandra came to my house the night before she was charged. She cried and said she’d meant to pay it back, that she had debts, that I didn’t understand. I told her I understood perfectly. I understood that my grandson had been humiliated over six dollars while she was spending money people gave specifically so that would never happen to any child.
She took a plea deal. Restitution and probation. The district recovered about half the money from her account, and the judge ordered her to repay the rest.

But the part that matters: when the story ran in the local paper, the town did something I’ll never forget. In two weeks, people donated enough through the district’s official account to wipe out every child’s lunch debt at every school in the county. Real receipts this time.
My grandson asked me why I was crying at breakfast. I told him it was because everyone’s lunch was paid for. He thought about it and said, “Even the kids who don’t have a grandma like you?”
